newsitem.title: UK: Moscow steals NATO's nuclear clothes to win debate.
newsitem.headline: Moscow steals NATO's nuclear clothes to win debate.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent
With a delicious sense of irony, Russia has stolen the West's Cold War nuclear strategy and is now using it as a weapon in the bitter fight against NATO enlargement.
The Soviet domination of Eastern Europe and the Warsaw Pact's vast armed superiority convinced NATO, from the 1950s, to rely on the power of nuclear arms.
Should the Soviet hordes make a grab for Western Europe, the idea was that nuclear weapons could and would be used -- first, if necessary -- to blunt the advance of such overwhelming forces.
Now, some senior Russian officials are deploying the same argument in reverse to conjure up a threatening picture of NATO as it plans to take in new members from Central and Eastern Europe.
Ivan Rybkin, secretary of the Russia's policy-making Security Council, signalled a possible shift to a more aggressive nuclear policy in a newspaper interview on Tuesday.
"Naturally we are not talking of a preventive nuclear strike but if an aggressor starts a war against us using conventional weapons, we may respond with nuclear ones," he said.

Western officials say his comments, while part of Russia's public and increasingly bitter campaign against NATO expansion, reflect a serious debate about the role of nuclear weapons in the defence of Russia.
The armed forces are in crisis following the disastrous defeat in Chechnya, a point alluded to by Rybkin. Morale is low and there is not enough money.
"There is a debate in Moscow about whether Russia's remaining nuclear capabilities should be used to plug the very real gaps in the country's security," said one Western military official.
"This is not just rhetoric, it's a serious issue," said Stephen Young of the British American Security Information Council (BASIC) in London.
"Perhaps they have no choice. There is, of course, no Western or NATO threat to Russia but there is a perception of threat, similar to the West's perception of the Soviet threat at one time."
Moscow's perception has some basis in reality.

Ten years ago, the Warsaw Pact still heavily outgunned NATO. A landmark arms control agreement on conventional forces in Europe, which put both sides on a more equal footing, was negotiated but not signed until 1990 as the Warsaw Pact fell apart.
Since then, Moscow has seen its empire collapse and once-firm allies clamour to join the old enemy's camp -- a spectacular shift in the military balance.
As a result, NATO has promised major revisions of the conventional forces treaty as part of efforts to reassure Russia that enlargement poses no threat.
A further irony is that the Soviet Union promised that it would, unlike NATO, never use nuclear weapons first in a conflict.
Russia's defence policy already envisages a more aggressive policy of using nuclear weapons first, providing it is facing a nuclear-armed opponent.
What Rybkin appeared to be saying is that Russia might move away even from that qualification and use nuclear weapons if attacked by any opponent.
Eric Arnett of the Stockholm International Peace Research Insitute (SIPRI) said Russia now spends a lot of money modernising its remaining nuclear weapons.

"This is partly the desire to maintain the status of military superpower, but there are those who want to rely more on the nuclear element to make up the conventional deficit -- as did the West," he said.
Even if Russia comes to rely more on classic ideas of deterrence, it is unlikely to mean a return to the old days of major East-West confrontation.
Both the United States and Russia have made deep cuts in their nuclear arsenals, and all short-range weapons for battlefield use have been withdrawn.

NATO has already promised that it will not station nuclear weapons on the soil of new member states in Eastern Europe during peacetime, although this has apparently done little to reassure the Russians.
